A risk is often expressed in terms of a combination of the consequences of an event (including changes in circumstances or knowledge) and the associated likelihood of occurrence.  \nWhere possible, try to combine similar risks to consolidate the number of potential risks.\t\t\t\t\t\n\tRISK IDENTIFICATION (SOURCE)\nThe purpose of risk identification is to find, recognise and describe risks that might prevent an organisation achieving its objectives.  When identifying risks the following questions should be considered;\n? What event(s) can happen that will have an adverse effect on the activity?\n? How can it happen?\n\t\t\t\t\t\n\tRISK IMPACT\nThe impact identifies the consequence of each risk (i.e. what are the effects to your organisation if it risk does happen?).\n\t\t\t\t\t\n\tRISK CONTROL\nA control is a current process, policy, device, practice or any other action designed to modify risk. Examples of controls include, checklists, meetings, procedures manual, contingency plans, audits and agreements in place.\n\t\t\t\t\t\n\tRISK TREATMENT\nA risk treatment is an additional activity being developed to manage and/or reduce the risk.  Examples of risk treatments include the creation of new guidelines, the introduction of a review process etc.  Once the proposed treatment has been implemented it becomes a control.\n\t\t\t\t\t\n\tEFFECTIVENESS OF RISK IDENTIFICATION\nAn adequate control implies that the risk is well managed and no further treatments are required.\nA marginally effective control implies that a treatment is not necessary however this may depend on the level of risk.\nAn inadequate control implies that treatments are necessary.\t\t\t\t\t\n\tLIKELIHOOD\nLikelihood is the chance that something might happen.  Likelihood can be defined, determined, or measured objectively or subjectively and can be expressed either qualitatively or quantitatively (using mathematics).\nRate the likelihood of the identified risk occurring with the controls in place.\nRatings are: Almost certain, Likely, Possible, Unlikely or Rare.\n\t\t\t\t\t\n\tCONSEQUENCE\nA consequence is the outcome of an event and has an effect on objectives. \nRate the consequence to the Project outcomes of the identified risk occurring with the controls in place.\nRatings are: Insignificant, Minor, Moderate, Major or Catastrophic.\n\t\t\t\t\t\n\t1Further information at: \tRisk Management - Principles and Guidelines 2018\t\t\t\t\n\tCURRENT RISK RATINGS\t\t\t\t\t\n\tLikelihood\tInsignificant Consequences\tMinor Consequences\tModerate Consequences\tMajor Consequences\tCatastrophic Consequences\n\tAlmost Certain\tLow\tMedium\tHigh\tExtreme\tExtreme\n\tLikely\tLow\tMedium\tHigh\tHigh\tExtreme\n\tPossible\tLow\tMedium\tMedium\tHigh\tExtreme\n\tUnlikely\tLow\tLow\tMedium\tMedium\tHigh\n\tRare\tLow\tLow\tMedium\tMedium\tMedium\n\tEXAMPLES OF RISK\t\t\t\t\t\n\tRisk\tLikelihood\nLow/Medium/High\n(comments)\tImpact\nLow/Medium/High\tMitigation Strategies\t\t\n\tDelays in receiving funding\te.g. Low\tHigh/Med/Low\tEnsure project deliverables are achieved in line with project plan and reported to the department in a timely fashion.\t\t\n\tDelays in recruitment of staff\tMay depend on nature, complexity and size of project.\tHigh/Med/Low\tRealistic understanding of what can be achieved within a limited timeframe and budget and awareness of what staff are likely to be available. \t\t\n\tBudget shortfalls\tProject has been appropriately scoped to cover all known contingencies. Project will be fully funded by Grant.\tHigh/Med/Low\tDevelop budgets to fully plan for known likelihoods and factor in relevant contingencies. Take a competitive approach to the market.\t\t\n\tBudget underspends \tWhere project is not rolled out in a timely fashion or has been inappropriately scoped in relation to expenditure. \tHigh/Med/Low\tEnsure a realistic project plan, timeline and budget are in place.\t\t\n\tOperational demands lead to delays to the timely delivery of project\tMay depend on scope of project; availability of appropriate staff; unforeseen circumstances; inadequate planning; unrealistic goals.\tHigh/Med/Low\tEnsure project manager/coordinator is fully capable and is working to a realistic project plan, timeline and budget can be enshrined in the Funding Agreement.\t\t\n\tCommunication with staff and/or target population\tInadequate or inappropriate methods of communication leads to breakdown in roll out of project.\tHigh/Med/Low\tCommunication with staff is incorporated into management plan along with a stakeholder engagement plan.\t\t\n\tTarget populations do not response to project\tLow uptake of project by target population.\tHigh/Med/Low\tThorough needs assessment and response is part of the project proposal and evidence of both need and adequacy of response is identified in project plan. This program aims to strengthen primary health \ncare by delivering funding to frontline primary health care services and improving the \naccess, delivery, quality and coordination of those services. This will help improve health \noutcomes for patients, particularly people with chronic and/or mental health conditions and \nassist in reducing unnecessary hospital visits and admissions. \nThe objectives of Program 1.6 Primary Health Care Quality and Coordination are: \n? \nimproving quality and coordination of primary health care \n? \nsupporting Primary Health Networks (PHNs) to increase the efficiency, \neffectiveness, accessibility and quality of primary health care services, particularly \nfor people at risk of poorer health outcomes, and improve care coordination and \nintegration \n? \nsupporting measures that improve the coordination and integration of health \nservices to manage health in the community, with a focus on complex and chronic \nconditions, and reduce potentially preventable hospital attendances and \nadmissions \n? \nsupporting the delivery of health information, advice and services through \ninformation communication technology to help people care for themselves and \ntheir families, and \n? \nsupporting the provision of high-quality palliative care in Australia through \nworkforce development, quality improvement and data development activities, and \nby supporting advanced care planning \nThe intended outcomes of the program are: \n? \nlocal needs are identified by PHN activities and initiatives are addressed \n? \nimproved quality of care for patients \n? \nimproved access to primary health care \n? \nimproved coordination of care for patients and integration of health services, and \n\n \nGrant Opportunity Guidelines ? GO8561 \n \n6  \n \n? \nthe needs of patients at risk of poor health outcomes are met through efficient and \neffective primary health care services \n2.1 \nAbout the Primary Health Network Program \nIn 2014-15 the Australian Government (the Government) selected organisations to \nestablish and operate 31 Primary Health Networks (PHN) through an open competitive \nfunding round. PHNs are independent, not-for-profit, regionally based organisations. They \nhave responsibility for undertaking data analysis and working with local communities, \nclinicians, service providers and state and local governments to identify and prioritise the \nhealth care needs of the population in their region. They commission health services to \nmeet the prioritised health care needs of their communities.  \nPHNs also play a key role in supporting general practice and other health service \nproviders to improve the integration of health services at the local level. In determining the \nregional boundaries of PHNs, several factors were considered including population size, \nLocal Hospital Network (LHN) or equivalent boundary alignment, state and territory \nborders, patient flow, stakeholder input and administrative efficiencies. This provided the \narchitecture to support joint planning, collaborative commissioning and health service \nintegration between Commonwealth and state and territory funded health services.  \nThe Government has identified seven key priority areas for PHN commissioning:  \n1. Mental health  \n2. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health  \n3. Population health  \n4. Health workforce  \n5. Digital health  \n6. Aged care  \n7. Alcohol and other drugs  \nAs regionally based commissioning organisations, the Government may also provide \nfunding to PHNs to commission other primary health care services, or provide sector \nsupport in the delivery of trials, time-limited activities, or the implementation of programs \nto support specific priorities identified by government.  \nThe PHN Program aims to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of medical services \nfor patients, particularly those at risk of poor health outcomes, and improve coordination of \ncare to ensure patients receive the right care in the right place at the right time.  \nThe objectives of the program are: \n? \nto improve the efficiency and effectiveness of health and medical services for \npatients, particularly those at risk of poor health outcomes, and  \n? \nto improve the coordination of care to ensure patients receive the right care, in the \nright place, at the right time.  \nThe intended outcomes of the program are to:  \n? \nensure local needs identified by PHN activities and initiatives are addressed  \n? \nimprove quality of care for patients  \n? \nimprove access to primary health care  \n? \nimprove coordination of care for patients and integration of health services, and  \n\n \nGrant Opportunity Guidelines ? The Australian Government committed to a new Commonwealth-wide \nframework to protect children and young people it is responsible for ? the Commonwealth \nChild Safe Framework (CCSF). \nThe Australian Government has put in place ways to apply certain child safety \nrequirements of the CCSF to grantees. A child safety clause will be included in a grant \nagreement where the Commonwealth considers the grant is for: \n? \nservices directly to children \n? \nactivities that involve contact with children that is a usual part of, and more than \nincidental to, the grant activity \n? \nactivities that involve possible contact with children that is irregular or unplanned. \nIf a proposed activity involves interaction with children applicants must comply with the \nAustralian Government?s Child Safety obligations. \nAt a minimum applicants must, in delivering the proposed activity, be compliant with all \nrelevant state, territory and Commonwealth law relating to employment or engagement of \nChild-Related Personnel. Where the activity involves planned interactions with children \ngrantees must also apply the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations, undertake \nan annual risk assessment of child safety and provide child safe training and education for \nstaff. \nPHNs will be provided with a template by the department to complete on an annual basis \nto report their compliance. This completed template will be provided to the department as \npart of their 12-month reporting which will be due 30 September annually. \n4.4.2 \nWorkplace Gender Equality Act 2012 \nThe Australian Government has a commitment to effectively support cultural change in \nAustralian workplaces and drive improved gender equality outcomes. Requirements have \nbeen implemented for fairer and more consistent measures to ensure the Government \n\n \nGrant Opportunity Guidelines ? GO8561 \n \n13  \n \ndeals with organisations who comply with the Workplace Gender Equality Act 2012 (the \nWGE Act). \nApplicants may need to satisfy a requirement to be compliant with the WGE Act. \nApplicants with 100 or more employees who are registered with the Workplace Gender \nEquality Agency (WGEA) and have been issued with a compliance letter are eligible to \napply for a grant. \nApplicants with 100 or more employees who are not registered with WGEA will need to \nregister to be issued with a registration outcome email prior to applying for a grant. \nApplicants with less than 100 employees across their entire structure who are \nunregistered, or have not previously reported to WGEA, or who do not meet the definition \nof a relevant employer under the Act, are not required to register. \nFor your grant application to be deemed compliant: \n? \nyour organisation must not be included on the WGEA website on the non-\ncompliant list \n? \nyou must be able to provide your registration letter or certificate of compliance to \nthe department if and when requested. \nIf you are unable to provide your certificate of compliance and/or appear on the non-\ncompliant list, you will be deemed non-compliant and withdrawn from the grant process. \nMore information regarding reporting requirements can be found at the Workplace Gender \nEquality Agency website. \n4.4.3 \nMulticultural Access and Equity Policy  \nThe Australian Government?s Multicultural Access and Equity Policy obliges Australian \nGovernment agencies to ensure their policies, programs and services - including those \nprovided by contractors and service delivery partners ? are accessible to, and deliver \nequitable outcomes for, people from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) \nbackgrounds.  \nGrant applicants should consider how they will ensure their services will be accessible to \npeople from CALD backgrounds.
